<reason>An elite, razor-close debate. B landed the single most dangerous attack: the motion grants weight by island category while justifying it by risk, so it is either arbitrary to islands or swamps them once all at-risk states qualify. But A met that pressure head-on in Rebuttal 2 with the "annihilation versus injury" distinction — existential risk as threat to state continuity, measured by share of territory rendered unlivable — which was prefigured in A's opening (habitability thresholds), not reverse-engineered on the spot, and it directly tracks the motion's own wording. B's "rigging" counter was sharp but absorbed in A's closing: population, GDP, and consensus all encode winners too, so the real comparison the motion demands is which currency fits what is being decided. On efficacy, A's empirical indictment of consensus (30 years, one 1.5°C sentence, blocked phase-out, a US Paris withdrawal under the rules B defends) was never factually rebutted; B's signature-as-accountability theory took real damage, while A's baseline-text mechanism (courts, border adjustments, finance conditions) was more articulated than B's bare assertion that those levers add nothing. Both sides were disciplined, well-grounded, and format-compliant; A simply left fewer live burdens unanswered.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 dilemma (island category vs. risk logic: arbitrary or swamped) was the debate's heaviest blow — and A's Rebuttal 2 A1 answer ("annihilation versus injury," total submergence as the limiting case of climate risk) was the debate's best answer, neutralizing the collapse charge and reframing B's strongest point as the criterion working as written.</best_rebuttal>
